For Viña del Sol I would recommend competitive benchmarking against its two direct Chilean rivals.

Internal benchmarking is cheapest and the data is already in-house, but the margin has been sliding for two years, so measuring the company against its own history only confirms the trend rather than showing what good looks like. The board asked for root causes; that won't give them any.

Functional benchmarking against the wider Latin American processing industry is a fairer comparison, but the product mix and scale differences would have to be normalised before any of the numbers meant anything, and that is a longer exercise than a board wanting answers this quarter will sit through.

Competitive benchmarking is the right call because the two rivals sell into the same market and work under the same Chilean food regulations, so any gap between them and Viña del Sol has to come from how the business is run rather than from circumstances management cannot control.

Viña del Sol's own gross margin has fallen from 38% to 31%, and on-time delivery is down to 74% against its 90% internal target. I would pull the two rivals' published margin and delivery figures and set them against those.

**Benchmarking Assessment for Viña del Sol**

**(a) APPLY — Evaluating the three methods against the scenario**

**Internal benchmarking** compares performance across Viña del Sol's own production lines or time periods. It is immediately accessible and low-cost, and may explain why gross margin has fallen from 38% to 31% — for example, by isolating whether the decline is concentrated in cold-press extraction or aseptic filling. However, internal benchmarking is self-referential: it reveals relative performance within the company but cannot establish whether 31% is competitive within the Chilean market or the broader industry. Given the strategic urgency of the margin decline, this limitation is significant.

**Competitive benchmarking** against the two Chilean rivals would be the most directly relevant approach, since both firms face the same input cost environment and distribution infrastructure. However, both competitors are privately held and publish no financial data, making detailed financial benchmarking difficult — though limited competitive benchmarking may still be possible using market intelligence, price comparisons, customer feedback and third-party industry data or trade association involvement. Management should not assume such data can be obtained.

**Functional (best-practice) benchmarking** compares Viña del Sol's cold-press and aseptic filling processes against best-in-class operators across Latin American food and beverage processing more broadly. Given that these processes are operationally transferable across the sector, Functional benchmarking is the most viable external route for process and delivery improvements, but margin erosion may also require commercial benchmarking of pricing, product mix and input costs — process benchmarking alone may not explain a margin decline driven by pricing or input inflation. It is the recommended primary method.

**(b) EVALUATE — Recommended approach**

A combined programme is most appropriate: internal benchmarking to establish a performance baseline and diagnose which lines are underperforming, followed by functional benchmarking to identify actionable improvement targets from comparable processors.

**(c) SCEPTICISM**

The board should confirm whether the gross margin decline reflects input cost inflation common across the sector rather than operational inefficiency — if so, competitive benchmarking data, were it available, might show that peers have experienced a similar decline, which would materially change the improvement priorities.
